projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Arthur Sibold was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: For the record, I would like your whole name.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Whole name, Arthur P. Sibold, S-I-B-O-L-D.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: And your birth date?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: August 18, 1920.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: For the time, I guess I am supposed to say Peter Glyer is making the recording with Art Sibold and I am just -- my wife works at Westminster and that's how I have come to get to know you. What branch of the service were you in?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I was in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: In the Navy?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Navy destroyer was the type of ship I was on. At least that's where I started out.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: That's where you started. What rank -- first, I guess it was the Second World War that you were in?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: World War II, right.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: World War II?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Um-hm.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What rank were you during World War II?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I went to the Naval Academy and graduated there and got an ensign's commission in 1942 and went aboard ship as an ensign and I stayed an ensign for six months or so and actually when I left the Navy, 26 years later, I was captain.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay. What -- when did you go to the academy? Was it in the late '30s?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: 1939 is when I entered.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So at that point, had the war in Europe looked like it was going to happen?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: The war looked like it was going to happen, but it had not started yet.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Why did you choose the Navy?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, it is hard to say. I guess I -- I don't know why I did it. It just seemed maybe a little more interesting than did the Army at the time. I had a couple of friends who had been in the Navy. And as a matter of fact, a couple of fellows who had been at the Naval Academy, first classmen visited us in Chattanooga and talked it up a bit and that's how I got interested in that. Also, it turns out that I was trying to get a free college education in those days and our congressman had an appointment at the Naval Academy, whereas he did not have one anywhere else. So I was able to get the appointment from him directly.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Now, was it a very hard competition to get into the academy?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: You had to take an examination and I would say the competition was, yes, rather tough. There was a lot of people who were flying, as there are today of course.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Right, right. So that where were you or what was happening on that Sunday in '41 in Pearl Harbor? What was it like to be at the academy and hear that was happening?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It is hard to say. I guess when I first heard it, they said the Navy had been attacked at Pearl Harbor. I didn't know where Pearl Harbor was to be perfectly honest. I was a pleb, I said pleb, I guess --

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: That's December '41?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: '41, maybe I was a youngster, sophomore. I wasn't real sure where Pearl Harbor was to be perfectly honest. It just had never crossed my mind. But it was -- it was of course quite a shock. But I remember the day very well. Bancroft Hall which was our dormitory at the Naval Academy.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Was everybody called into formation and you talked?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, no, no.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It just sort of went on?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It happened there. Everybody had been listening to the radios and following the news broadcasts and so forth. I don't remember there being any particular big event that occurred there, an admiral talking to us, announcing it to us or anything. I don't remember that.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Was there a change in the rate at which they then moved you through the academy?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Oh, yes. We -- our -- the immediate plan was to cut our four-year curriculum to three years and they did that. They eliminated things like languages and English and history, things that you didn't really need. They concentrated on gunnery, seamanship, navigation and the things that are unique to a Naval officer. Those courses they kept and they speeded them up. We went to a six day a week and eliminated all vacations. We didn't have any time off to speak of.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So there weren't any summer cruises?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, they eliminated the summer cruises. I did have one the first year I was there. But the second year, I was supposed to take a destroyer cruise and they eliminated that entirely. We just stayed there and kept studying.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So they really could get the three years?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: They compressed everything into three years. We missed some stuff. Some of the languages, particularly. I think languages is something that has been neglected. They should have had more of that.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: To sort of go ahead a little bit, did they ever have a plan that after the war, that they would bring you back and give you some of that or --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, no. They just --

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It was just lost?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: You would pick it up, make up for it in working hard at sea. And no, there was never any talk about coming back and having any more time.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You would probably have a bunch of rebellious kids on their hands?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I'm sure, yeah, yeah. At that time, having been in the fleet and operated as officer, why, we weren't about to come back and go to school again, I assume.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What was life like at the academy in that early time period when you were going to school? What was --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It is hard to say. Everything was speeded up. As I mentioned, they eliminated vacations. We just didn't have any vacations anymore between terms and stuff like that. Summer vacation, we didn't have. It was just hectic and busy. We worked hard and did --

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did discipline change at all?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, discipline didn't change.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It was always stiff and continued stiff?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Continued stiff, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did some of the traditions that they had, you know, the upper classmen getting to --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Hazing and stuff like that?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Haze and forth?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I don't recall any of that slackening at all. It was about the same throughout.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Except as a third year, you were top dog?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: As third year or fourth year, you didn't have to put up with hazing. It was only the plebs that got hazed.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Do you remember any of the training experiences while you were there?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: The what, training?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Training experiences while you were there?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, I went with the gunnery training particularly.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What did they do?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: They took us down to the armory and we would learn about the guns, how to train them, fire them. We didn't fire them at the Naval Academy but we, you know, elevated -- set up the guns in the operator's seats and operated the guns, got familiar with the parts of the gun. Of course we were studying the mechanisms all the time, so we got to know how they operated.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So that they had some -- I will call them dry mounted 5-inch, 3-inch and 4, 4s and forth?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: All the things that we were going to encounter in the fleet, they had copies of them in the armary and we got familiar with them to that extent.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay. Do you remember any of your instructors?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Not really. At this point, I have forgotten them. I could I guess rack my brain and come up with some names.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Maybe more in terms of their characteristics or, there was someone who was always --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, there were -- I just don't remember the instructors very well at all. They were very competent fellows. They were, of course, officers, lieutenants and -- lieutenants, most of them.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: How well did you feel that the academy prepared you for your first ship?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, it -- I think did a very fine job and I have an interesting little story. When I went aboard ship, the first ship I was assigned to was the Wainwright which was a destroyer squadron, flag ship, and it had a commodore on it, it was a -- Captain D.P. Moon, Don Pardee Moon.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes. I know of him?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: You know of him really?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes, he was involved at Normandy and --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yes, he was.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: And the Med?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, Okay. I was on his ship.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: And it is funny, we -- after graduation from the Naval Academy, I was trying to find my ship. I knew the name of the ship and they told me to go to Norfolk and report to the receiving station and wait for the ship to come in. Well, I did that and when I got to Norfolk, why they said the ship was not coming in, go to New York. So they sent know New York and I got to New York and they said the ship is not coming in here, go to Boston. In those days, ship movements were highly classified. So nobody would tell you anything about where they were. They would say go to this place and wait. After chasing the ship for a number of months, oh, maybe two months, I finally made contact with it at New York Harbor. By that time, the ship had been on the Murmansk convoys.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Oh, cold?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, I missed the Murmansk convoys, but when they got back, they started transferring a lot of people. The people who had been on the ship for a while were going to go to new construction ships. So those of us who were brand new had to get assignments and fill in for the guys who were getting promoted and moved off other ships. One of the people who got transferred was the executive officer immediately and they moved the gunnery officer up to the executive officer's job, leaving vacancies in the gunnery job. Well, they started looking around for a gunnery officer and the man who was normally assigned to that job who would have been assigned was a fellow named Frank Sellers. He was the class of '42, one year ahead of me at the Naval Academy, senior to me, and he would have gotten the department head of the ship. Except the admiral, the commodore heard that he had been the anchor man, anchor man meaning last man to graduate. He just barely got buy. So Captain, Commodore Moon said, hell no, I am not going to have the anchor man as my gunnery officer on my flag ship, find somebody else. Well, I was the only guy who had any gunnery training at all. We had a number of ROTC officers from Yale, Harvard, for instance, and so forth but they hadn't had any practical gunnery experience. So I was the only one I guess qualified for the job, so I got it. By virtue of the fact that the others were not qualified and the fact that the fellow who would have gotten it was the anchor man, the commodore wouldn't stand for him having the job.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: That's quite a bit of responsibility for someone just fresh out.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It was, and I was very fortunate we went straight to Casablanca, the landing over there, and I was put up as gun director and I was there directing the gun fire support for shooting at the French destroyers and shore batteries right out of the Naval Academy, and I did get a commendation for that from the fleet admirable, the action reports mentioned that I had fresh caught and was in that job, so I did get a Navy commendation ribbon for that.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: That's the only citation I ever got during the war. I did get it fairly early.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: That was November of --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: '42, November '42 it was, yes.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: How large a fleet was off Casablanca?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, it was about six destroyers and the battleship Massachusetts. They sent the Massachusetts over there because the French had had their battleship the Jean Bart was being built in Casablanca and I guess there was some doubt whether the Jean Bart would get under way, and if they did, they wanted an American battleship able to take it on. It turns out the Jean Bart was not able to shoot or move. It was tied up in the harbor and couldn't have done a thing. So we had one battleship and five or six destroyers was the Navy force.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So you were -- that constituted the fire support?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, we fired at the beach. We had some French destroyers there tried to exit the harbor and come back and attack us, but we chased them back in. So it was an exciting little battle there. Of course the German airplanes came over and bombed us at night.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did they?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: That was sort of exciting at the very beginning too.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What procedures would you have used for protection of the fleet when the German aircraft coming over?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, we tried to -- it was night, the Germans couldn't see us. They dropped flares and tried to locate us that way, but we could try to hide under the flare which would blind them. They couldn't see us and our skipper wouldn't let us shoot at the German airplanes for fear of giving away our position. So we didn't do much fighting at the airplanes. I wanted to, I wanted to shoot one down right away, but we didn't get a chance.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So you went -- after joining the Wainwright, what sort of ship was the Wainwright, was a destroyer itself?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It was a destroyer, yes.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What class destroyer?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Sims-class. Sims-class destroyer.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Was it a four stacker?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It was a one stacker. It was built just before the war or at least that was the class -- probably the last class that was completed before the war was started.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What was the characteristics of that kind of ship?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It had five 5-inch guns, but it was top heavy. So they took off one of the 5-inch guns to give it more stability so it wouldn't roll so far. It was just a plain old destroyer.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What was it, a complement of about 200 men?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: 250, men something like that. Maybe 20 officers. We had a -- yeah, 20 officers. Another thing that was interesting, aboard ship the officers, most of the officers on the ship were from Yale, Harvard, Princeton, the Ivy League officers, ROTC officers, and they had graduated or commissioned those officers about two weeks ahead of the Naval academy people. So when I got aboard, I was the junior officer and we didn't have enough state rooms for us. So I had to sleep in one -- a lounge, and I always felt it was, I got shafted there. I didn't have a state room. The ROTC officers did.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Despite you being the gunnery officer?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, well, yeah, yeah. Theoretically, I don't think they really designated me as gunnery officer that young. I was gun director, doing the gunnery officer's job. But I don't think they called me gunnery officer at that point. I was just main battery officer.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay, okay. How well did the men bond as a unit on a ship like the Wainwright?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, I thought we had very wonderful core there, a fine group of officers -- enlisted men, of which I still remain in contact with some of them.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Do you?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I go -- I used to go to the ship reunions they had down in Norfolk, and I went to those for four or five years. We have had one up here in Washington. But it was a fine group of young men.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So you stayed with the Wainwright for a long time?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I stayed with the Wainwright for about five years.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Through the whole of the war?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: The whole war. It was only --

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Interesting.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I rode from the Wainwright toward the end of the war, the destroyers were getting clobbered out in the Pacific, the kamikazes. Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: And the Wainwright was sent out there to replace some of those that have been damaged. I rode as far as Pearl Harbor before I got transferred to another ship the Cory which was under construction at the time. So I never did get to the Pacific war at all. But -- I never really got to the Cory because before I got to the Cory, I was transferred to another ship, the Shea, a mine layer, a destroyer mine layer. So that was the extent of the seagoing experience.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So you were telling me before, in a -- before this interview that you spent an awful lot of time in the Med.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yes, we did a lot of convoying over there. Convoying to Casablanca, first of all, and then immediately we started resupply convoys to Sicily and Anzio and Salerno and places like that. Up and down the coast of Algeria and Tunisia and so forth.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did you participate in other invasions in the Med that would be Casablanca, Sicily, Anzio?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, all of those.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: All of them?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: The only one we didn't participate in was southern France which was the one that took place right after D Day.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes, in August of '44?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: August of '44, yes.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: And you were just doing convoy duty at that point?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Convoy duty and whenever there was a landing schedule, they would send us over there and we would peel off and join the shore bombardment. We spent a lot of time in the city of Palermo up there, right after it was captured by the Americans and we were first destroyers to get up there, our ship. We got heavily bombed up there by the Germans.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes, I would imagine.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: They tried to drive us out but we stayed there and supported Patton and his groups, his troops, and they crossed over trying to drive the Germans out of Sicily.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Typically in working shore bombardment, and I gather you did a lot of that, was there -- how were the plans worked out for that kind of support? Did you put radio operators on the shore? How did you-

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, we just had charts showing where the targets were and when we went up to support a landing, we really didn't have much of an idea as to what we were going to be shooting at, but we sort of would shoot at targets of opportunity and we would get some -- the people down below in CIC used to get directions as to where to shoot. I was a gun director. I didn't know what the target was really.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You just pointed and shot?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Pointed and shot, and it would spot us and tell us to change to the right or left or up or down to try to get the targets.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: How were the plans worked out for that kind of support? Did you put radio operators on the shore? How did you --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, we just had charts showing where the targets were and when we went up to support a landing, we really didn't have much of an idea as to what we were going to be shooting at, but we sort of would shoot at targets of opportunity and we would get some -- the people down below in CIC used to get directions where to shoot. I was a gun director. I didn't know what the target was really.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You just pointed and shot?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Pointed and shot and would support -- you know, they would tell us change to the right or left or up or down to try to get the targets. But we had a lot of gun fire support there in Salerno, Anzio and Sicily, and that was it.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did you participate in the Normandy landings?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, we didn't.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So you just stayed in the Med?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We stayed in the Med. I thought certainly -- since we spent so much time over there, I thought we would be part of the Normandy invasion, but we didn't. We were not part of it. We were running convoys to England mostly.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Were you?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: At that time.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Typically -- tell me about a convoy experience. You picked a convoy, a group of ships up in a harbor like Casablanca or Palermo?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We would pick them up in New York City.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay, then --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We would form -- we had submarine warfare around the convoy and we would shepherd them across the ocean to where we were headed, England or some places in the Mediterranean and we lost some ships over there, the submarines would get through occasionally, and torpedo them. So we saw a lot of sinkings up there, but nearly not as bad as at Murmansk Run which were really tough for the guys up there.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Typically how many ships would be in a convoy and how many ships would be on escort?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It would be eight or nine ships on escort and probably 60 or 70 merchant ships in the convoy.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Would you form lines from the outside?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: A circle. Sort of a half circle around the convoy protecting it as they moved through the water, you know, protected the forward end.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay, as opposed to someone guarding the tail end?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We had some destroyers that would -- they would be assigned to the tail end to keep submarines from sneaking up.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: And get the back side?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: In the rear, yeah. But usually we were going fast enough that submarines didn't have much of an opportunity to catch us on the surface and they couldn't make the speeds needed under water. So we didn't have any problem with coming up from stern.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: When did aircraft carriers, the baby flat tops appear?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I didn't operate them.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You did not have those?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I don't remember any convoys that we had flat tops, air cover at all. They were there with other convoys but not with ours.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Not with yours?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Not with ours.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Because yours were fast enough?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, not necessarily that, but I guess we didn't take them to where they were -- I don't know. I don't --

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You didn't operate?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We didn't operate with carriers, American carriers.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did you ever have aircraft over head for any period of time?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Occasionally we would have these antisubmarine aircraft just looking, flying out to keep the Germans from operating on the surface. Just enough air cover to discourage them from operating on the surface.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Catalinas and --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Bigger-- yeah, long range patrol planes. But there weren't a lot of them, not very many.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Not very many?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, not to my recollection.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So most of your time then was spent on convoy duty?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Most of the time was spent on convoy duty.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You must have crossed the Atlantic a lot of times?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Eight or ten times I suppose. Something like that.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: How long would it take you to go across?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Oh, ten, twelve days. We would turn around and come back right away. We didn't waste any time over there.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did you escort back or was it --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We brought ships back, yes, but they were empty of course, but --

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Therefore able to go faster?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, I don't recall they went much faster. But I guess they did. They would have been able to go faster, maybe one or two knots faster. But we had to -- we didn't want to lose the empty ships. We needed them.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Sure. When you would come into port with convoy duty, did you typically stay a week or was it immediately right back?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, most of us, most of the ships, our destroyers went in for overhaul or for a short period of maintenance in the shipyard. We were New York shipyard, Boston shipyard or Portland, Maine or someplace like that where we could get repairs made and there are always some things that needed to be worked on that the ships' force couldn't take care of. So we would say maybe two weeks.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It was one of those periods that I got married up there.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Oh, really? Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, after I first landing the Casablanca, I decided, having gotten shot at a bit, time had come to get married real quick. So I called up this girl that I was going with at Hollings College and I asked her to marry me and she accepted. So we met up in New York City and we were married in St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York City.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: In fact, I was just there.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: You were?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We were -- when I say the cathedral, we were in the rectory which was next door to the cathedral. In those days, non-Catholics -- my wife is non-Catholic. Non-Catholics could not be married in the church, so we had to be married in the rectory. But we were married by a Catholic priest. We did that on a three-day weekend up there.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Holy cow. And then reported right back to the ship?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Right back to the ship, yeah. We may have been there another week or so.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did she come up with you to the ship or did she go back home?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: She stayed there in New York City for a couple of days and then went on back home. She was living with her mother in Alexandria while I was overseas.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So if you got to down to Norfolk, maybe you might get close?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, drive up to Alexandria was nothing at all.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Of the ports in the Med, what do you remember about them?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I remember Palermo port very well because that's where I say we got bombed regularly by the German bombers coming over at night. As soon as they found out we were in the harbor, they would come over and drop flares and try to locate us and then bomb us but we were able to avoid being hit over there. Only thing, one ship did get hit was the ship Franklin Delano Roosevelt, Jr., was on. The president's son was on the one of the ships, destroyers in our squadron, and his ship took a bomb right down the stack.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: That was a little bit of excitement. That was the only ship that got hit over there. It was exciting to, you know -- you couldn't see the German bombers. You could hear them and you could have them on radar, but you couldn't tell where they were and the skipper wouldn't let us shoot at them, so it was --

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So he sort of maintained that policy all the way through?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Don't fire at them?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Pretty much, yeah. Occasionally we would get off -- we would have an opportunity to shoot at them, but we didn't hit anything. It was firing sort of blind up in the air.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: When did you get radar? That was something that came in during the war?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Radar came in very early during the war and our ship was one of the first destroyers to get it. And we were learning how to use it at that point in time, tactics, how to use radar tactically. But it was exciting to be able to see what radar could do for you, navigation and ship detection and so forth. We felt pretty confident we could spot German submarines on the surface. I'm not sure we could have. We felt we could. So we had -- we tried to keep a real sharp eye. We certainly didn't want to lose any ships that were under our care at the time. And our commodore was -- he was a tough nut. I always said he was the Navy's equivalent to George S. Patton. He was a real hard nose guy and made it real tough on the -- our flag ship.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did your ship always remain as the flag?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: The whole time I was there, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: The whole time?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Admiral Moon, Captain Moon finally was transferred, as you said. He went to Commander of the Naval Forces at Utah Beach at Normandy and eventually right after D Day occurred, they transferred him and his force down to Naples. While I was in Naples, he committed suicide.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Did you know that?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: I knew that.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: You knew that. Well, I -- I happened to make contact with his communications officer and I asked him, I told him I had been on Moon's flag ship and could he tell me why, what caused him, how did Moon die. He told me gave me the full story of how he committed suicide there in Naples because he was so distraught about losing some destroyers at Utah Beach and also he was the commander at Slapton Sands. Have you ever heard of Slapton Sands?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: That's where the LST's got clobbered by the German torpedo boats and he felt very responsible for allowing that to occur. And he was expecting to get court marshaled for that and consequently he committed suicide.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It is unfortunate because I understand he was a very good officer.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: He was a fine officer. Hard to get along with, but, you know --

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What kind of contact did you have with him, as long as we are talking about Admiral Moon, what -- here you are, fresh --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I was standing -- I was officer on the deck watches up on the bridge and the bridge was where he hung out all the time under way. So he was on the bridge all the time, and it was just, you know, he was keeping an eye on everybody on the ship. So you really, on your -- you did things right up there, you didn't go to sleep on watch. You acted alert and tried to do your best because you were under his observation all the time. One interesting thing is right after Casablanca, we were escorting the battleship Massachusetts back to the States after we decided to bring her home and we were up ahead of the Massachusetts submarine screen. It changed course and the captain at that time was down in the ward room having supper or having dinner in the ward room when they changed course and the standard practice is for the officer of the deck to tell the captain he has to receive orders to change course. He passed the word to the captain, the captain said, oh, it is a simple change, so he didn't go to the bridge to observe the change in course. It turns out this young officer up there on the bridge cut right across the bow of the Massachusetts and we almost got sunk, rammed by the Massachusetts.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: That must have been --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I tell you they set off the collision alarm and everyone went flying to the bridge. Captain Moon had his quarters one deck above the ward room. So he got to the bridge ahead of the captain and when he got there and found the captain was not on the bridge in this crisis situation, he put him in hack which means he relieved him of command right away and made the executive officer, made the gunnery officer -- the executive officer skipper temporarily. The captain was forbidden to the to go to the bridge. It is the first time I ever heard of that. But Moon was a tough nut and he was -- he was going to punish the captain right away for not being present when all this occurred. It really -- it was an exciting time.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So you were right in the middle of the Atlantic and almost got cut in half?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Almost. I didn't see the Massachusetts, but we heeled over, turned sharp and fast, and people who did see it said we almost got clobbered right there, rammed by the Massachusetts that would have been the end of the Wainwright and possibly all of us on board. Other ships that were rammed had collisions and were sunk of course during the war. We were very lucky at that point.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did the same group of ships that were in this squadron basically stay together the whole time?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Stayed together the whole time. Occasionally they would peel one off for some special operation but most of the time -- we weren't a full squadron. Normally, a full squadron I think is nine destroyers. We only had about six that were operating together all the time, and the other three were maybe in the Pacific or something.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay, so it wasn't as if someone was off getting repairs while -- sort of a rotation?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, these six stayed together pretty much all the time. We went to the shipyard together and came out together and took many convoys together.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Were they all basically the same class?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, there was another -- the other class was --

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Fletcher?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, it wasn't Fletcher. Fletcher was a later class. I forget the other class. They were also signal stackers, but an older class ship.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So you kept the older ones in the -- Atlantic?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Old ones in the Atlantic and all the new ones, new construction went to the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did officers and men sort of come and go off your ship sort of to give experienced blood to some of the new construction?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: That's right. We lost, oh, maybe 20 percent of our crew every time we came in port, being transferred to the new construction ships and that was just standard practice since you had to -- you were training people all the time, big turnover in personnel.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay, but never you? Until you went to Pearl --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I was, I guess forced -- I stayed with the Wainwright until the end of the war, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: That's amazing.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You must have got to know that rusty bucket quite well.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did it have any peculiar characteristics? They always talk about a personality of a ship.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I don't recall any particular personality or traits of the ship or the crew. It was a good ship. We had good skippers and this captain who was put in hack, he got transferred eventually of course, but he was replaced by a fellow who had been teaching submarine warfare back here in Washington. So when we sank our submarine we had the new skipper on board who was a real experienced -- and a submarine warfare man. He was the one who was in command when we sank the German submarine.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You did sink --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We sank one in the Mediterranean, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: When you were in on convoy duty?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, I forget -- we were sort of on special duty looking for -- we knew there were submarines around there. They had torpedoed a couple of American destroyers about that time. So they put us on patrol trying to find this German submarine that was doing the damage and we happened to stumble across it along with a Calpe, was it British or South American, anyway, there was another destroyer with us, British, a British destroyer. The two of us together teamed up to sink this German submarine, the 593.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: One come and then the other come in?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: One would stand off and ping on him and then direct the other one where to go. So we would take turns depth charging it.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did your ship jump when you would drop the charges?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, we could tell -- it shook. It didn't jump. We were steaming pretty fast when we fired the depth charges to get out of the way. We didn't want to get blasted, blast ourselves in the water. So we were steaming pretty fast.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Would they come just off the end or did they also come off the sides?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Come off the sides. You would roll them off the stern. We got pretty proficient at dropping depth charges, believe me.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Now, did you stay as the gunnery or main control officer the whole time through or did you have other assignments on the ship?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, I was a gunnery officer when I left, when I was transferred.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yes, I was. But we didn't have any gunnery exercises in the Pacific, of course. We only got as far as Hawaii before I got transferred. So I didn't have a chance to go to Iwo Jima or one of those places where they did a lot of shooting.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family, with your wife and so forth?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I wrote her letters. That was about it. Of course whenever we hit port, why, whenever we would hit port, she would generally be there. It was interesting, she had a good friend whose father was in Navy operations at the Pentagon and he knew I was on the Wainwright. He couldn't tell her when the ship was coming in, but he would password to Connie, his daughter, tell Livie to go get her hair done, which meant that the Wainwright was coming in port soon and she would be getting a phone call. So she would generally wait until I called her up and she would come to Norfolk or Boston or Portland, Maine or wherever.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: She would travel by train?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Travel by train, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Was that -- was it -- train is never convenient, especially at a time when everybody is --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: They were loaded in those days with traveling people, soldiers moving them back and forth. Of course there were no airlines flying at that time.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes. And was it easy to get housing?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Not housing, no.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Not -- but you would at least be able to see each other for the week or two weeks when you --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We would find a place to stay in whatever port we were in, motels and whatever.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Sure, sure. You would have to obviously go, report back --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I was still on -- I had to report back every day. So I was going back to the ship in the morning and coming back home at night.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It must have been nice.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It was. It was good, newly married.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: And what was food like on the Wainwright?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, since it was the flag ship, we had a pretty good officer's mess. We had good stewards on there taking care of the commodore, Captain Moon, and the same ones doing the cooking for the ward room. So we had pretty good food.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It sounds like you did.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No complaints.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You know they always talk about Navy coffee can stand your spoon up.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. Midnight watch, had coffee going all the time in the ward room of course.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So would be on watch four on, four off?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, four on, four off, except doing the dog watch. That's four on and two off or two on and four off, I guess it was. I am sorry, I have got a -- I am getting hoarse here.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Was there anything that you would do every time you would go out to sea for good luck?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It was just --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Just say my prayers and hope to come home, the only thing.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did you have any, either on ship, on board ship or in port, European ports or back home, any particular humorous events?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I guess the nearest thing, being gunnery officer, I used to hold loading drills on our loading machine. Every ship has a loading machine where the gun crew practices shoving projectiles in the gun and powder in the gun, and simulating firing. When you are in action, you want to shoot real fast and effectively. So you had to do a lot of practicing with the physical handling of the shells, and dummy shells and dummy powder, and one time I guess I got the officers, challenged the officers to take on the best gun crew to see who could load the fastest. I got my hand caught in the breach and smashed a finger and I got a Purple Heart for my gun crew. They gave me a -- made a great big purple heart to hang on my damaged hand.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: As I recall, they would sometimes award a ship the letter E.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: E for efficiency in operations and steaming -- I forget what they called. It was steam play, more miles per gallon, that kind of thing.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did the Wainwright receive any such awards?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, we had -- I think we had an E for gunnery efficiency or something like that maybe at one point in time. (Pause)

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: 99, starting on side two of the tape. Where did we leave off. I got so excited about punching the tape. We were talking about the funny experiences and the efficiency and so forth. Did you have competition between -- you end up having four main guns, two forward and two aft?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, we didn't have competition. At least I don't recall any competition like that. We just -- we had gunnery exercises and we just made sure that all the guns could fire pretty fast, pretty fast. We didn't time them or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It was more -- how would you zero the guns, go for accuracy? How did you do all of that to make sure that the -- that you are going to hit what you needed to hit?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, my recollection was that when we finished a shipyard overhaul, why, the ordnance people in the yard aligned the guns, all the guns on one target. So that when we left the yard, they were properly aligned and we tried to keep them aligned until we got back the next time.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay. Did you did your ship -- characteristically, things are going to wear out. But did it, was it always a propulsion system that have more finicky than anything else or the radar system or the other kinds? Why would -- what were the most common kind of repairs?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I don't remember very many casualties on the Wainwright. We had a pretty well-trained crew. Most of those guys, at least the senior chiefs and petty officers on there, had been on the ship a good while and kept things in pretty good shape. We had some good people on there. And I just don't recall any casualties at that point. I can't think of a single one. Obviously, we had some. I guess the radar was -- would go down occasionally and we would have to -- but we had a good technician on there who could fix it and get it back on the air again.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: When the -- before you had radar and then after you had radar, was there a difference in the way the ship operated or the way they configured it so that now you had to go around? Did it -- did it change or alter the way the ship functioned?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Not to my knowledge, no. Being in the gun director, I don't know what went on down in CIC. Obviously there was some changes down there, but I was not close enough to that operation to say. We were all learning how to make good use of the radar and there was a brand new technique that was coming in and we were particularly interested in those features that would help us detect German submarines on the surface. The Germans would snorkel at night and we tried to keep a good sharp lookout for the small pips that would come up with the snorkel. But we were fairly successful in keeping them at bay.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Keeping them down?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, keeping them down. That applies to the whole U.S. Navy at that point. Everybody was learning the same thing. As I say, we were fortunate, we had this Captain Strobane who had been teaching submarine warfare to crews here in the states, so he was right on top of all the latest techniques and ways of fooling the submarines and sneaking up on them and so forth.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Interesting.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: He was a good man.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So Strobane took over for the captain that got hacked on --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did he stay with you for the remainder of the time?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: He got transferred eventually, too, and I forget the names of the other skippers.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You had several --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Several skippers, every 18 months we would get a new skipper. Turning, you know, a lot of -- building a lot of new ships and they had a -- they had to have a lot of trained officers experienced officers --

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: To go to --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Go to the ships.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Go to the new ships and so forth?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: After Moon left, did you get a new commodore?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yes, we did. I don't remember his name.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So just -- those also changed the same periodically?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yes, periodically they would change.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You would get command changes?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay. Did you, obviously we don't have any here tonight, but did you ever take photographs or anything of that time frame?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, cameras were not allowed aboard ship. And the one time we wish we had photographs was the time we sank the submarine, but it turns out the officer who had the camera was left on the beach when we sailed. We sailed quickly from one of the ports in North Africa to chase a submarine and we were not -- unable to make contact with the officer who had the camera, so he got left ashore. So we didn't have any cameras aboard ship to take pictures. Fortunately the Calpe, the ship we were with had some pictures, and in my folder over here, I have a few pictures that they took.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Oh, do you? Did you keep a diary?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, I did not.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It would be more through your letters home that you could vaguely constitute a diary at this point?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I don't think I could constitute a diary at this point. I don't know if my wife saved those letters or not. I suppose she did, but I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What did you think of fellow officers who were on board?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I was very much impressed with the quality of the Ivy League officers we had. As I say, most of them came through the Ivy League; Princeton, Harvard, Yale, Columbia, so forth. They were good officers, very good officers.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: How long did it take your ROTC officer, trained officer to come up to academy standard -- if there was a difference between the kind of knowledge, craftsman, sea craftsmanship and so forth?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Oh, yeah, three or four months at sea would do it. I guess the one thing that I remember was different, when I went aboard ship, I was put on officer of the deck watch right away. I think they had to go through two or three weeks of training because they had not had preliminary experience which I had gotten at the Naval Academy. They caught up with us where they could carry their load in a couple of months I would say. But they were good officers, smart guys. Unfortunately, I didn't maintain -- I really haven't. But first reunions we went to, I tried to maintain contact with them as much as I could. But they didn't have the interest in going to reunions that I did, so, you know, I don't correspond with them at all now.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Do you remember, were there particular friends that you had among that group?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. I particularly remember a fellow went to Gettysburg College. He was my best man.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: At our wedding in New York, yeah. I can't come up with his name. Hewell, I think it was. What his first name was, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Just ward room chums?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Ward room chums, yeah. Some of them were rather from rather prominent families in Boston. Fullam, Jerry Fullam. The name doesn't mean anything to you, I'm sure. The name didn't mean anything to me, but they were a big prominent family in Boston in the fish business, the Fullam fish market up there.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: After the war, why did you decide to stay?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Stay in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yeah. I mean, you could have gotten out, a lot of people did.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I could have but I was enjoying it at that point in time. I thought it was great. I thoroughly enjoyed my time in the Navy. The Navy had sent me to MIT for radar training, electronics training. So I had an electrical engineering degree from MIT, which was working toward an engineering duty assignment at ship yards and laboratories, and that was particularly interesting. So I guess that's what kept me in. My last years in the Navy were served as an engineering duty officer.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Were they?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, except for the first few years at sea, I didn't go to sea at all.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You had all the sea you needed?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So when you came back and first the Korea, then off to this mine land destroyer but never even saw it come down the ways?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What sort of assignments did you have after the war if you were to sort of layout your career?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, okay. I went to Charleston Naval Shipyard as an electronic officer down there or electronics shop, yeah, electronic shop officer, and then back to the bureau of ships here in Washington, and then went to the Armed Forces special weapons project at Albuquerque which is the atomic weapons project out there. I guess the last tour was with commander and chief of the Pacific fleet staff out there, electronics ships staff. So I had some good shore duty after the war ended. And it was the good prospects of good shore duty that kept me in I think at that point. I had hoped that I would be given a command of a shipyard, but I didn't ever get that.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: The Navy though did send you for extra schooling in terms of going to MIT? That was what, about a year's time?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: About a year and a half up there at MIT.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What year was that?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So really soon after the war?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, '48 and '49. That was right when the Navy -- the Navy was just getting a lot of radars installed in the ships and they needed people with radar training, particularly which they had not had before, so they set up a special course at MIT for radar training and assigned some of us to go up there and get a concentrated dose of it. And then sent out us to laboratories and shipyards.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: To teach others or --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Teach others and monitor the work that was going on, keep things moving in the radar field and sonar. Sonar was another, you know, underwater sound. That was really my specialty underwater sound.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Was it?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So that you, were you involved in some of the land base systems which we had for listening under water?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: To some extent, yeah. To some extent. The laboratory where -- under water sound laboratory at New London, they were really the sponsors of the new system which is the big net. It was all over the world where we track Russian submarines wherever they are. Long range detection of submarines. It is a very powerful system. In effect, we are able to track German submarine, Russian submarines wherever they go.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Anybody's subs?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Anybody's subs, yeah. That was an exciting field, particularly the -- did you ever see the movie or read the book Hunt for Red October?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, a lot of that stuff was what we were doing, under water sound laboratory, the kind of capabilities that were displayed in that movie, long range detection and tracking and so forth.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Did you ever have occasion to go, even though you did not have sea duty, to, as part of the lab or as part of your other assignments, land assignments to go out on ships to check out some of the newer equipment or --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Off and on, yeah. Up in New London, we were right across the river from the Groton shipyard where they were building submarines and occasionally we would get to go aboard those and there were a lot of other submarines up there. So we would ride them occasionally out in the Long Island Sound. We never made any long-range cruises on them, at least I didn't.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: How different was it being under, like you were on the other side?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I wasn't -- I -- looking back on it, I wish I had gotten into submarines when I graduated. I had a choice of asking for submarines or destroyers or whatever, so I asked for destroyers and got it. But some of my classmates went into submarines. Of course a lot of them sunk, they didn't come back, but submarine was -- submarine warfare, submarine service is certainly the prime duty of the Navy these days.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It certainly is, yes.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Those fellows contributed an awful lot to putting it to the Russians.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You talk about having gotten together with some reunions. Tell me a little about those.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, one of the -- let me see. The reunions basically were reunions of the crew, the enlisted men, and it was rare that officers went to those reunions. However, I decided I was going to go to them because I had such -- a lot of good friends who were going, good friends on the ship so I did go. We had them down in Norfolk and I guess I went to -- we had a couple out in Bloomington, Indiana. Yeah. It was a nice experience to bump into those guys 15 years later and guys you had known -- I never -- I wasn't real close friends with very much many of them, but there were a couple of them who were my gun captains on the ship that went and particularly this fellow from Pennsylvania now calls me occasionally on the telephone. He is a Cherokee Indian, but he was one of my gun captains. So we have a lot of laughs about old days on the Wainwright there.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Is he about the only one that you really stay in contact with?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: About the only one I stay in contact with. The others, a lot of them have died.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What was the average age of the crew on the Wainwright?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Oh, 20, 21, 22, something like that.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Just a bunch of kids.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, a bunch of kids.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Were the officers not much older?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: That's right, the officers were not much older.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You had a captain who was the daddy of the ship and a bunch of kids just having fun, playing games?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: It was a mighty serious game?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: It was. I had a real good friend from North Carolina who was on this -- we both got assigned to the same squadron at graduation. He was on the Rowan. I was on the Wainwright. We were both in the same squadron. And unfortunately, the Rowan got torpedoed at I guess Anzio, he was lost, a good friend of mine. He and I used to bum around on the East Coast together when we would get in port. A real good fellow. I guess that was my best friend lost at sea. We didn't have any casualties at all that I can think of on the Wainwright. We were lucky. We didn't get into any serious accident, shell hit and that sort of stuff. Casablanca, we could have been hit by some of those big shells. The French had, the Vichy French had a big shore Battery El Hank, which was down the coast from the Casablanca and it was fighting with the battleship Massachusetts. Both of them had big guns and they were shooting at each other, but they were not interested in firing at us, we were too little.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: And too nimble?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yes, zig-zagging around, trying to dodge shells.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: If you were to try to explain to someone who was not there in World War II, how would you capture what was it really like in those times? How would you describe that?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Hm, well, I would say it was hectic but it was exciting. I mean, we were busy all the time and we were always under the threat of being torpedoed or, you know, our lives were at risk to some extent. Not greatly at risk, but it was tense at times. But we were lucky. We didn't have casualties, that sort of thing. Some of our other ships did get hit.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: In the squadron?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: In the squadron, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Is that because your ship being the not the capital ship but --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: The flag ship.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: -- the flag ship was not in as much action?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, generally our commodore and captain would have mixed it up along with all the rest of them.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What was it -- just luck of the draw?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Luck of draw. We didn't happen to be there when the bombs were falling in that spot. As I say, the ship that FDR, Junior was on, they got hit. There was a number of casualties on their ship. But the other ships in the squadron, I think just like ourselves didn't have casualties at all except for the Rowan.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Have you talked with your children or your grandchildren about the experience at all?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: No, not really. Not really.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Have they been curious or --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We chat about it occasionally but not -- we haven't sat down like we are doing today and talk about it in detail. They have never raised any questions. My son was in the Navy and he, I think, pretty well understood what was going on and he didn't need to be told what it was like. But -- as a matter of fact, I had two sons in the Navy, which brings up an interesting little point, I will tell you, it has nothing to do with this. The Naval Academy, alumni magazine, Shipmate, this thing they put out every month for the alumni and a couple of months ago, it was a feature article in there on the Battle of Wei, remember the city Wei?

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes, I do.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: The North Vietnamese had captured the city and pretty much taken over and the marines were sent in to recapture and drive them out and the man -- the officer in charge of that marine operation was named Bob Black. It turns out he was my son's first classman at the Naval Academy, a pleb goes in and he is generally assigned a first classman sort of picks him up.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: A mentor?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Mentor. So every pleb has a first classman and every first classman has a pleb. So Bob Black and my son were first class and pleb. Bob Black, as I say, was in charge of this Wei marine operation and they were fighting for their lives out there in the city of Wei about to be overrun by the North Vietnamese. So Bob Black had to call in gun fire support from the Navy ships that were offshore there. So he put in his request for help and they sent him an -- assigned a ship to him, the Lynn McCormick, it turns out it was my son's ship and my son was gunnery officer on that ship. So the pleb was firing gun fire support for the first classman. They didn't know it. At the time they didn't know it. He didn't find out that Brian Siebold was the gunnery officer on the ship that I'll say saved his neck. Maybe I am stretching the point, maybe it didn't save his neck.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Brought some comfort.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Comfort. Sure did. Interesting little coincidence.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Yes, but gunnery officer also?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: He was a gunnery officer on the Lynn McCormick.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Interesting.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, we got a lot of gunnery training here at the Naval Academy. So the ROTC officers, they didn't have the hardware on the campus to train. So what training they had to get, they had to wait until they got aboard ship. Here at the Naval Academy, they had it already.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Is a gunnery officer one of the positions of prominence or --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yeah, I would say so, yeah, captain, second and gunnery officer -- or operations officer and gunnery. He is number four, I guess, in line of command generally. Rather important position on a destroyer.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay. On almost any --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Almost any ship, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: How fast could your ship go?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I think we could make about 30 knots.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: But not that often?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Not -- it burned up too much fuel. It was not an efficient way to travel.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Thirty knots was about the most. We were a pretty fast ship when we got going. I think I mentioned the ships initially had five 5-inch guns. But when we put them to sea, they turned out to be top heavy, so we had to remove one of the guns to reduce the heavy metacentric height and make it a little more stable, so they took off one of the guns so we only had four guns on most of those ships.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: So it was originally two forward, three back and then you ended up --

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Two forward, two back and one midship, something like that.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: They took off the midship?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I think it was the midship gun that went off.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: How effective -- you had, what, five inch guns fore and aft and then what were the lighter -- all the way down to 20 mm?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: 20 millimeters and 40 millimeters were the anti-aircraft guns we had.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Dual force Bofors?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Bofors, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: You could put out quite a shield of steel?

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: We thought we could. I'm not sure how effective it was. It was basically just -- it was like shooting ducks. You try to lead the guest, lead the target, and they didn't have very good gun sites in those days, so help track them. So you were putting out a lot of lead hoping they ran into it.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Plus the fact that you're turning and twisting. You get a good lead and suddenly the ship leans the other way.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: What haven't I asked you that I should be asking you, either experience or just anything.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: I wouldn't be able to tell you if I could think of. I had some tidbits I wanted to get in there and I told you about those. I can't think of anything.

sp.speaker: Peter Glyer
sp.p: Okay. Well, then we will call this interview to an end. I do thank you for your time.

sp.speaker: Arthur Sibold
sp.p: Well, okay, I have enjoyed talking to you and baring my soul, whatever.
